title: Gun Fever

jokes.text: 'You're such a dildo, dude.' 'Thanks, dude. Thanks. That's a good way to start the day.'
jokes.setup: Mac insults Dennis by calling him a dildo first thing in the morning
jokes.punchline: Dennis thanks him as if it's a compliment, then sarcastically notes it's a great way to start the day — total deadpan acceptance of the insult
jokes.explanation: A solid cold-open joke that efficiently establishes the casual cruelty of these friendships. The deadpan acceptance is funnier than outrage would be. Not exceptional but sets tone well.

jokes.text: 'Is that soy veggie health drink supposed to erase the damage you did to your liver last night?'
jokes.setup: Dennis is drinking a healthy smoothie in the morning
jokes.punchline: Mac points out the futility — a health drink can't undo a night of liver-destroying drinking
jokes.explanation: A functional observational joke about health-conscious people who also drink heavily. Competent but familiar territory — this joke has been made in many forms before.

jokes.text: 'If you lowered your standards a bit, you'd get laid more.'
jokes.setup: Dennis objects to Mac's judgment about the woman Mac slept with
jokes.punchline: Mac defends his behavior by advising Dennis to lower his standards — framing promiscuity with ugly people as aspirational wisdom
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy — Mac delivering unsolicited life wisdom that is both self-incriminating and genuinely terrible advice. The confidence with which he says it is very Mac. Decent quotability.

jokes.text: Dennis refuses to let Mac sip his health drink because he doesn't know what diseases the woman Mac slept with has.
jokes.setup: Mac wants to try Dennis's healthy drink; Dennis refuses because Mac made fun of it
jokes.punchline: Dennis escalates the reason: not just spite, but because he doesn't know what diseases Mac might have contracted from the woman — connecting the drink to STD contamination
jokes.explanation: The punchline adds a satisfying second layer — moving from petty refusal to a gross STD implication. The structure is clean: expected reason subverted by a weirder, funnier one. Good economy.

jokes.text: 'There's been a B&E, dude.' 'A what?' 'A B&E, dude!' 'A B&E?' 'What does that mean?' 'Breaking and entering.' 'No. No!'
jokes.setup: Charlie urgently announces a B&E at the bar
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis are so clueless they don't know what B&E means — and when they finally get the answer (breaking and entering), someone still says 'No. No!' as if rejecting the definition
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy showing the gang's collective incompetence. The confusion about 'B&E' paired with someone rejecting the correct answer is funny and character-specific. The repetition builds well.

jokes.text: After a prolonged argument about whose fault it is, Mac's decisive solution to the robbery is: 'We need to buy a gun.'
jokes.setup: The gang is yelling about whose fault the robbery is; someone intervenes saying they need to be rational
jokes.punchline: The 'rational' solution Mac proposes is immediately buying a gun — both a character reveal and an absurd non-sequitur to 'be rational'
jokes.explanation: This is a tight structural joke — 'we need to be rational' creates an expectation of measured thinking, then Mac's punchline ('we need to buy a gun') perfectly subverts it while also being entirely in character. The economy is excellent: the entire joke's premise and payoff is delivered in two beats. It also sets the episode's plot in motion, which is good writing beyond just the joke.

jokes.text: Well, it's somebody's fault. / I know it's somebody's fault! / Well, it's somebody's fault! / I know that!
jokes.setup: The gang is trying to figure out who's responsible for the robbery
jokes.punchline: The 'argument' devolves into everyone just repeating 'it's somebody's fault' back and forth with increasing volume — zero productive content, pure ego clash
jokes.explanation: Classic Sunny gang dysfunction where the conversation produces no information. Functional but not especially inventive — more of a character texture beat than a crafted joke.

jokes.text: The detective tells them to get a safe 'that a relatively small man can't just carry away.'
jokes.setup: The gang reports the robbery to the detective expecting meaningful help
jokes.punchline: The detective's only advice is about safe size — delivered flatly, suggesting this is the full extent of police assistance
jokes.explanation: Solid deadpan from the detective — the specificity of 'relatively small man' makes it funnier than just 'bigger safe.' Establishes the institutional indifference that motivates the gang's vigilante subplot.

jokes.text: 'Not really.' 'What in the hell does that even mean? How could there not be any leads?'
jokes.setup: Dennis asks if police have any leads on the robbery
jokes.punchline: The detective's non-answer 'not really' sends Dennis into an indignant spiral — his outrage at police incompetence is both justified and completely over-the-top given these characters have no moral authority
jokes.explanation: Functional joke about police indifference meeting civilian outrage. The irony that these terrible people are demanding competent law enforcement is there but undersold.

jokes.text: Hey, babe. / Hey, Colin. [lingering kiss/greeting]
jokes.setup: The gang has been having a serious conversation about robbery and gun safety when Dee's boyfriend Colin waltzes in
jokes.punchline: The intrusion of a romantic moment into a tense conversation, with the gang presumably staring uncomfortably — the visual awkwardness of Colin's arrival cutting off serious discussion
jokes.explanation: More of a tonal beat than a crafted joke — the interruption is funny contextually but there's not much comedic architecture here beyond the incongruity of the romantic moment.

jokes.text: 'Dude, your sister has the worst taste in men.' 'No shit. I hate that guy. He's like a full-on '80s movie stereotype.'
jokes.setup: Colin, Dee's boyfriend, has just left after being unhelpful and smooth-talking
jokes.punchline: Dennis dismisses Colin as an '80s movie stereotype' — a specific and sharp piece of pop-culture-grounded character mockery
jokes.explanation: '80s movie stereotype' is a sharp, specific character read — it's the kind of observational comedy that feels true and is delivered with genuine contempt. The two-step (worst taste in men → I hate that guy → specific diagnosis) is well-paced.

jokes.text: Mac reveals Colin has been 'dating every hot bartender in town' and was seen 'hand all down the back of her pants' with someone else a week ago — while Colin is currently dating Dee.
jokes.setup: Dennis dismisses Colin as a stereotype; Mac ups the ante
jokes.punchline: The specific detail of 'hand all down the back of her pants' is gleefully grotesque — escalating from 'player' to a vivid image of public groping
jokes.explanation: The specificity of the physical detail elevates this above a simple 'he's a cheater' revelation. Also plants the Colin-as-villain plot. The 'Oh! Gross. Very gross.' reactions suggest this lands well on screen.

jokes.text: That guy's dated, like, every hot bartender in town. I saw him a week ago with Wendy from Dirty Frank's. Hand all down the back of her pants.
jokes.setup: Mac is building a case for why Colin is a bad guy
jokes.punchline: The specific detail of 'hand all down the back of her pants' is gratuitously physical — Mac's indignation is about Colin's player behavior, but the vivid specificity of his memory is funnier than the moral outrage
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Wendy from Dirty Frank's' grounds the absurdity in Philly's bar world. 'Hand all down the back of her pants' is a memorable detail. Solid comedic beat.

jokes.text: 'Mac gets a boner every single time he thinks about a gun.'
jokes.setup: Dee is asked whether Mac and Dennis will actually buy a gun
jokes.punchline: Dee's explanation reduces Mac's enthusiasm for guns to a purely sexual response — 'gets a boner every single time'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. The sexual framing of Mac's gun obsession is both funny and psychologically pointed — it foreshadows the episode's theme about guns as a masculine fantasy. Dee delivers it with perfect deadpan. Highly quotable. 'Gets a boner every single time he thinks about a gun' has the rhythm of a great character-defining line.

jokes.text: Dee says owning and knowing how to use a firearm 'is an important part of what makes this country great' and that 'there's nothing sexier than when you're firing a gun. It really turns me on.'
jokes.setup: Dee is in a talking-head; we expect her to agree with her earlier skepticism about the gun
jokes.punchline: Instead, she gives a pro-gun speech that escalates from patriotic talking point to pure sexual arousal — completely undermining her 'no guns' stance from the prior scene
jokes.explanation: The pivot from NRA talking point to 'it really turns me on' is a great structural move — the first half sounds sincere, the second half reveals the actual motivation is sexual. Dee's hypocrisy about the gun is funny and consistent with the show's theme that everyone is compromised by their own desires.

jokes.text: There's nothing sexier than when you're firing a gun. / Actually, it really turns me on.
jokes.setup: Colin is enthusiastically endorsing gun ownership to Dee
jokes.punchline: He pivots from patriotic rationale to straight-up sexual arousal from gun firing — echoing and confirming Dee's earlier observation about Mac, but applied to the villain
jokes.explanation: This mirrors Dee's earlier line about Mac, deepening the thematic joke that gun fever is literally sexual. The escalation from patriotism to arousal in one breath is well-timed. Solid character comedy with a callback dimension.

jokes.text: Mac to Dee: 'Well, that's exactly why I want you to teach me how to use one, sexy.' Dee's flirtatious response is immediately deflated: 'You've got a poppy seed in your teeth.'
jokes.setup: Dee and Mac are flirting over the gun; Mac calls her 'sexy' and proposes she teach him — a charged romantic-comedy moment building
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately points out he has a poppy seed in his teeth, destroying the moment with mundane physical reality
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural deflation. The scene builds romantic tension — 'sexy,' 'it would be my pleasure,' 'the pleasure would be all mine' — then the poppy seed lands as a complete tonal reset. It's economical, surprising, and character-appropriate (Dee's obliviousness to social moment-killing). The specificity of 'poppy seed' rather than just 'food' makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Mac stares into space apparently trying to remove the poppy seed while Dee watches awkwardly, then tells him 'It's a big one. You might wanna go to the bathroom.'
jokes.setup: The poppy seed has killed the romantic moment; Mac is presumably probing his teeth
jokes.punchline: The extended beat of Mac fumbling with his teeth while Dee watches is uncomfortable, then she escalates: 'It's a big one' — further humiliating him
jokes.explanation: Extension of the poppy seed joke — the callback works ('it's a big one' escalates the humiliation) but it's diminishing returns. The awkward beat of Mac presumably picking his teeth is implied cringe comedy that plays on screen.

jokes.text: Charlie trying to calm down his landlord Hwang while Hwang screams about $854 in back rent and Charlie offers him a Rice Krispie treat.
jokes.setup: Hwang is furious about overdue rent; Charlie tries to defuse the situation
jokes.punchline: Charlie's response to an enraged creditor demanding $854 is to offer a Rice Krispie treat — the most pathetic and inappropriate de-escalation possible
jokes.explanation: The Rice Krispie treat offer is a brilliant piece of character comedy — it's so specifically Charlie (impoverished, feckless, trying to charm his way out of problems with the most pitiable possible gesture). The disproportion between the demand ($854, Hwang screaming) and the response (Rice Krispie treat) is perfect. This is very much a Charlie joke.

jokes.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah! Calm down! All right! / Hwang. You're just in time, buddy. / Charlie, my rent!
jokes.setup: Charlie is introduced dealing with his landlord Hwang, who is aggressively demanding rent
jokes.punchline: Charlie's completely transparent stalling ('you're just in time, buddy!') while clearly having no money whatsoever — the cheerful greeting to someone he owes money to
jokes.explanation: Charlie's haplessness with money and his bizarre optimism in the face of an angry creditor is good character work. 'You're just in time, buddy!' to your angry landlord is very Charlie. Competent character comedy.

jokes.text: 'I can't wait too long! Hwang not patient!'
jokes.setup: Hwang is waiting for Charlie to retrieve money
jokes.punchline: Hwang refers to himself in the third person — 'Hwang not patient' — an absurd grammatical choice that's both funny and characterizing
jokes.explanation: Third-person self-reference is a reliable comedy beat; 'Hwang not patient' has good rhythm. The character is a type (angry Asian landlord) that the show uses somewhat broadly, which limits the originality score.

jokes.text: 'I placed a couple bad investments. It could happen to anyone, right?'
jokes.setup: Charlie is unable to pay rent; Hwang is threatening him
jokes.punchline: Charlie's explanation for not having rent money is 'a couple bad investments' — delivered as if this is a reasonable explanation from a reasonable person, when Charlie clearly has no investments and no money
jokes.explanation: Charlie's self-delusion is a core character trait and 'bad investments' captures it perfectly — the gap between his self-image as a business person and the reality of being a broke bar nobody is very funny. 'It could happen to anyone, right?' adds perfect defensive pathos.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis stash the gun and immediately agree they should never touch it — then immediately ask if they want to shoot it.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis solemnly declare the gun will only be for emergencies and 'hopefully we never have to pick it up again'
jokes.punchline: Without pause: 'You wanna shoot it?' 'Yes.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural joke. The setup (solemn, responsible gun storage speech) is punctured with maximum economy — the punchline is literally five words total. The timing is everything: the gap between 'hopefully we never pick it up again' and 'you wanna shoot it?' is probably about two seconds. This is a textbook example of comedy economy and character hypocrisy delivered with perfect rhythm. Among the episode's best.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis gleefully shooting a log in the woods and shouting 'You totally killed that log, dude!' 'I totally killed it. I always knew I'd be good at this stuff.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are testing out their gun in the woods
jokes.punchline: Their targets are logs; they celebrate killing a log as if it's a triumph of marksmanship — grown men acting like children with a deadly weapon
jokes.explanation: The childish celebration of killing a log is very funny — it shows these men have the emotional maturity of 12-year-olds with a new toy. 'I always knew I'd be good at this stuff' from Dennis is a great piece of narcissistic character work.

jokes.text: 'If that log was trying to rob the place, you would have killed it.' 'I would have killed it!' 'You totally would have killed it!'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are praising each other's shooting of a log
jokes.punchline: The hypothetical scenario of a log robbing a place — and the genuine pride they take in defeating this imaginary threat — is delightfully absurd
jokes.explanation: The absurdist logic of 'if that log was trying to rob the place' is unexpected and funny — it reveals that Mac and Dennis are not thinking about actual self-defense scenarios but fantasizing about heroic violence against even inanimate objects. The mutual reinforcement of this delusion is very funny.

jokes.text: Charlie arrives and lectures Mac and Dennis about gun safety in a serious tone, then immediately asks 'You wanna hold it?' — and Charlie initially refuses, then immediately says 'Fine. Give me the gun. Fine. Yes. I'll hold the gun.'
jokes.setup: Charlie scolds the guys for playing with the gun and says they need to open the bar
jokes.punchline: Charlie's moral objection evaporates the instant he's offered the gun — the same hypocrisy as Mac and Dennis stashing the gun
jokes.explanation: This mirrors the earlier stash-and-shoot joke, extending it to Charlie and making it a running gag about no one having actual gun discipline. The escalation of Charlie's capitulation ('No... Fine. Give me the gun.') plays well.

jokes.text: That's not fun! That's not a toy. / Oh, come on, Charlie.
jokes.setup: Charlie catches Mac and Dennis playing with the gun like children in the woods
jokes.punchline: Charlie — the most irresponsible member of the gang — is the voice of gun safety, which is ironic and funny given he'll acquire gun fever moments later
jokes.explanation: The irony is good — Charlie, who will catch 'gun fever' in about 60 seconds, is currently the responsible one. Gets rewatch value. Good setup for his character arc in the scene.

jokes.text: 'Is this thing loaded?' 'It can be.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is holding the gun for the first time, feeling it out
jokes.punchline: His innocent question 'is this thing loaded?' gets the ominous, non-reassuring answer 'it can be' — which is somehow more alarming than 'yes'
jokes.explanation: Four words total. 'It can be' is funnier than 'yes' because it's both an evasion and a threat — it implies Mac might load it right now, depending on his mood. The nonchalance of the answer is perfectly timed. Excellent economy.

jokes.text: Charlie shoots the gun, then Mac and Dennis celebrate with 'That's my boy!' and 'Whoo!' and immediately start asking him to describe what he feels.
jokes.setup: Charlie shoots the gun for the first time
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis's homoerotic excitement at Charlie firing the gun — 'that's my boy!' 'describe what you feel' — frames the gun as a sexual initiation ritual
jokes.explanation: The guns-as-sexuality theme that Dee established earlier is extended here through Mac and Dennis's weirdly intimate enthusiasm. 'Describe what you feel' is particularly funny in context. Good character integration.

jokes.text: 'I feel focused and I feel badass and just... badass, you know?'
jokes.setup: Mac asks Charlie to describe the feeling of firing the gun
jokes.punchline: Charlie's attempt at eloquence collapses into repeating 'badass' — he doesn't have the vocabulary to describe the experience but he's entirely earnest
jokes.explanation: Very Charlie — the inarticulate doubling back to 'badass' because he doesn't have more words is both funny and sad. It's perfect character integration: Charlie is not good with language, and when he has an overwhelming feeling, he just says the same word twice.

jokes.text: 'Charlie, my boy, you've got the gun fever.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has just shot the gun and is visibly affected
jokes.punchline: Mac diagnoses him with 'the gun fever' — a fake condition that Mac clearly invented, delivered with the gravity of a diagnosis
jokes.explanation: The title drop doubles as a great joke — Mac's invented diagnosis of 'gun fever' as if it's a real affliction is perfectly in character (Mac loves to feel like an authority). The phrase is quotable, provides the episode title, and captures the show's thesis about how guns seduce people. Highly memorable.

jokes.text: That is sexy. / Yep, totally. / You feeling sexy?
jokes.setup: Charlie has just been diagnosed with gun fever and is clearly excited
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis declare Charlie's gun enthusiasm 'sexy' and ask if he's 'feeling sexy' — the sexual undertone of gun ownership made explicit between friends with no self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Reinforces the episode's theme of guns-as-sexuality. Mac and Dennis don't realize they're confirming Dee's observation. Good thematic callback but not a great standalone joke.

jokes.text: Dee tries to escalate the flirtation further ('Well, actually, I've got something I think you'll love') and Mac cuts her off: 'I'd rather watch you shoot the gun here.'
jokes.setup: Dee is trying to reciprocate Mac's sexual interest with her own proposition
jokes.punchline: Mac shuts it down — he'd literally rather watch her fire the gun than engage in whatever she was offering. The gun IS the sexual experience for him.
jokes.explanation: This is the payoff of Dee's gun-arousal gag combined with Mac's established gun obsession. Mac preferring gun-watching to whatever Dee was proposing is a great character-specific joke that actually says something about Mac's sexuality. The deflation is well-structured.

jokes.text: 'That's true. Wanna go shoot it some more?' 'Yes! Let's do that.'
jokes.setup: Mac has just laid out a plan to investigate the robbery 'with the gun'
jokes.punchline: Dennis immediately loses the thread of the investigation plan and pivots to shooting the gun again — 'wanna go shoot it some more?' with zero transition
jokes.explanation: Another beat of the running gag: they keep inventing excuses to shoot the gun and abandoning any responsible use of it. The speed of Dennis's pivot from 'investigate' to 'shoot it more' is funny.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis discover the gun is gone from the stash and immediately know it was Charlie, then call him — Charlie casually confirms 'Yeah, I got the gun.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis go to retrieve the gun and find it missing
jokes.punchline: Without needing any investigation, they immediately know it's Charlie — and Charlie doesn't deny it, as if taking the bar's gun to handle his landlord situation is perfectly normal
jokes.explanation: The speed of their deduction (they just know it's Charlie without explanation) is funny — it implies Charlie is exactly the kind of person who would take their gun. Charlie's nonchalant 'yeah, I got the gun' treats this as completely reasonable.

jokes.text: 'Is this the gun fever talking, dude?'
jokes.setup: Charlie has taken the gun and Mac is trying to understand why
jokes.punchline: Mac invokes 'the gun fever' as an explanation — his invented condition now being used as an actual psychological framework
jokes.explanation: Good callback — Mac using 'gun fever' as if it's a legitimate diagnosis is very in character and extends the joke well. The phrase has legs.

jokes.text: Charlie, apparently holding a gun, offers Hwang a Rice Krispie treat again when Hwang comes back demanding his rent money.
jokes.setup: Hwang has returned demanding his money; last time Charlie offered Rice Krispie treats
jokes.punchline: Charlie offers Rice Krispie treats again — this time possibly while armed, making the offer even more absurd and weirdly threatening
jokes.explanation: The Rice Krispie treat callback lands well because we now know Charlie has a gun — the juxtaposition of the most pathetic possible negotiating tool (a snack) with the most dangerous one (a firearm) is very funny. The running gag has escalated.

jokes.text: Hwang's threat trails off mid-sentence: 'Hwang will be forced to...' [long pause] 'I'm sorry. Forced to...' [another pause] — Hwang cannot figure out what his threat is.
jokes.setup: Hwang is delivering a threat to Charlie about consequences for not paying rent
jokes.punchline: Hwang cannot complete his own threat — he doesn't know what he would do, suggesting he has no actual power over Charlie
jokes.explanation: This is a great escalation-to-deflation joke. Hwang's blustering authority is completely punctured by his inability to finish his own threat. The double pause ('Forced to... I'm sorry. Forced to...') extends the discomfort for maximum effect. This is very much an IASIP joke about impotent authority figures.

jokes.text: While Hwang struggles to complete his threat, Charlie is apparently doing something with the gun — Hwang sees it and his demeanor changes completely, saying 'What you doing? What's that?'
jokes.setup: Hwang is mid-threat; Charlie has the gun
jokes.punchline: The implied visual of Charlie casually handling the gun while his landlord threatens him — causing the landlord's bravado to instantly evaporate — is a dark, funny moment about how guns change power dynamics
jokes.explanation: This is the dark heart of the episode's gun theme — Charlie using the gun's mere presence (not an explicit threat) to cow his landlord. The comedy is in Charlie's obliviousness to how threatening this appears versus how threatening he actually means to be. 'What you doing? What's that?' captures Hwang's terror perfectly. Great dark comedy.

jokes.text: 'I have my ways. Do you know what I mean, Hwang, when I say I have my ways?' [pause] 'What is that? Is that a yes?'
jokes.setup: Charlie is calmly explaining to a terrified Hwang that he'll get the money because 'he has his ways'
jokes.punchline: Charlie's cartoonish gangster phrasing ('I have my ways') while apparently holding a gun — and then his confusion about whether Hwang's terrified non-verbal response counts as a 'yes' — is a perfect Charlie moment
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Charlie using movie-gangster language ('I have my ways') while being completely oblivious to how terrifying the situation is — and then needing verbal confirmation from his traumatized landlord — is pitch-perfect character comedy. It's funny because Charlie thinks he's being clever and diplomatic, not threatening. The 'Is that a yes?' in particular is excellent: Charlie's earnestness in the face of Hwang's probable terror.

jokes.text: Say yes if you know what I mean when I say I have my ways. / Yes. / Oh, good boy. Get lost.
jokes.setup: Charlie has demanded verbal confirmation from Hwang about understanding his vague threat
jokes.punchline: 'Good boy. Get lost.' — Charlie dismissing his own landlord like a child after extracting a meaningless confirmation, completely inverting the power dynamic
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. 'Good boy. Get lost.' directed at your landlord who is owed $854 is perfectly absurd. The economy is exceptional — four words that invert a power dynamic completely. Charlie treating his creditor like a dismissed subordinate is a perfect encapsulation of his delusional self-image. Strong candidate for best individual line in the episode.

jokes.text: 'Sometimes I can't understand you. You're talking, but I don't understand you.'
jokes.setup: Hwang is apparently making sounds or non-verbal responses while terrified
jokes.punchline: Charlie's complaint that he can't understand Hwang — when Hwang is probably incoherent with fear — is oblivious to the point of being almost surreal
jokes.explanation: Charlie's obliviousness continues — he's frustrated that the terrified man he's accidentally threatening won't communicate clearly. Very much in character. The joke has diminishing returns at this point in the Hwang scene but still lands.

jokes.text: After getting a terrified nod from Hwang, Charlie concludes the conversation with: 'Oh, good boy. Get lost.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has gotten Hwang's (terrified) agreement that Charlie 'has his ways'
jokes.punchline: 'Oh, good boy. Get lost.' — Charlie's dismissal of his own landlord, treating Hwang like a misbehaving pet, is a remarkable inversion of the power dynamic
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's sharpest line. 'Good boy. Get lost.' — four words — is stunning in its economy and character revelation. Charlie, who is broke and inarticulate, has accidentally terrorized his landlord with a gun and then uses the authority this has given him to dismiss the man who owns his building like a disobedient dog. It's dark, it's character-perfect, and it's delivered with the casual confidence of someone who doesn't realize how absurd they are. This clears the bar for an 8+ score.

jokes.text: Sometimes I can't understand you. You're talking, but I don't understand you.
jokes.setup: Hwang has apparently said something in response to Charlie's 'my ways' speech
jokes.punchline: Charlie's complaint that he can't understand Hwang — delivered while Charlie is the one making zero sense and Hwang is the one with legitimate grievances — is perfectly inverted self-unawareness
jokes.explanation: The inversion is good — Charlie, the incoherent one, complaining about Hwang's communication is a solid ironic joke. Good character-specific moment.

jokes.text: 'This is great, dude. We're like the Hardy Boys.' Mac claims to be Frank Hardy because 'Frank was kind of the leader.' Dennis says Frank had blond hair and therefore he should be Frank. They argue about this for thirty seconds.
jokes.setup: Mac invokes the Hardy Boys as a template for their detective work
jokes.punchline: The argument about who gets to be Frank Hardy — a pointless debate about a fictional character's hair color versus leadership — reveals their complete inability to focus on anything that matters
jokes.explanation: Classic IASIP structure: a dumb argument that reveals character. Mac's argument is about authority/leadership; Dennis's argument is about appearance/vanity. Both are completely wrong-headed. The Hardy Boys reference as an aspirational detective model for two incompetent adults is funny. The argument runs a bit long but is in character.

jokes.text: Didn't Frank have blond hair? / Yeah. But that doesn't make any difference... / So I should be Frank 'cause I have lighter... / The hair color doesn't matter.
jokes.setup: Mac has claimed to be Frank Hardy because Frank was the leader
jokes.punchline: Dennis tries to claim Frank based on hair color — an entirely different and equally irrelevant criterion — while Mac insists it's about leadership, not aesthetics. Both are arguing about a fictional boys' book series
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the Hardy Boys argument is excellent character comedy — Dennis's counter-claim based on hair color (shifting to vanity from Mac's leadership argument) is perfectly in character for Dennis and perfectly absurd. These two are arguing about identity politics within a fictional boys' detective duo instead of investigating a real robbery.

jokes.text: 'Or we could call your sister to do her job... that is if she's not having sex with Colin and every other bartender in Philadelphia.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis debate whether to open the bar before investigating
jokes.punchline: Mac casually speculates about Dee's sex life — to her brother Dennis — with zero filter
jokes.explanation: Mac's casual oversharing about Dee's sex life to her brother is nicely cringe. Dennis's reaction ('Don't do that. It's gross.') is funnier than the line itself. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: 'Holy shit! I know who stole our safe!' Mac's sudden realization mid-argument, followed by them immediately running off with their detective kit.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis have been bickering and unable to focus; then Mac suddenly has a revelation
jokes.punchline: The comedic whiplash from pointless Hardy Boys argument to sudden revelation is funny; the speed with which they grab the ziplock bags and run is very much in keeping with their impulsive characters
jokes.explanation: The pivot is funny but not exceptional. The best part is that their elaborate detective kit (bags, Maglite) is immediately abandoned in the rush, suggesting their preparation was entirely performative.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis arrive at Charlie's apartment and Dennis immediately says 'Oh, this place is a shit-hole, Charlie. It smells.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis come to Charlie's to get the gun; Charlie asks if they want to know who did it
jokes.punchline: Dennis ignores Charlie's revelation and leads with complaining about Charlie's apartment — his vanity and class snobbery trumps any interest in the actual crime
jokes.explanation: Dennis's disgust at Charlie's apartment is in character for his snobbery, and the timing (prioritizing the smell over the solved robbery) reveals his narcissism. Solid but not exceptional character comedy.

jokes.text: Mac's plan to confront the suspect: 'I'll slide the gun meaningfully into the front of my pants.' 'I know that game.' 'Yeah.'
jokes.setup: The gang has decided Colin is the thief and they discuss how to handle it
jokes.punchline: Mac's tactical plan is to 'slide the gun meaningfully into the front of his pants' — which he treats as a known strategy ('I know that game') — implying this is a recognized intimidation technique from their shared cultural vocabulary
jokes.explanation: 'Slide the gun meaningfully into the front of my pants' is a very funny phrase — the word 'meaningfully' does a lot of work, implying a kind of choreographed menace. Dennis's 'I know that game' is a great straight-man confirmation that this is somehow a culturally agreed-upon move. Very much IASIP energy.

jokes.text: Hey, Dee. Are you with Colin right now? / Oh, no. He had to meet someone at Fingers Bar, huh? / Nice.
jokes.setup: Mac is on the phone with Dee, fishing for Colin's location
jokes.punchline: Mac's satisfied 'nice' upon learning Colin is at a bar that's already been robbed — his plan is coming together
jokes.explanation: Minor plot-advancing beat with a small comedic payoff in Mac's self-satisfied 'nice.' Not a crafted joke so much as a character tone moment.

jokes.text: Mac attempts to put the gun in his waistband and fumbles with it; someone says 'It goes... Uh, stick it back in...' and there's an extended beat of Mac struggling with the gun.
jokes.setup: Mac's big intimidating move is to 'slide the gun meaningfully' into his waistband
jokes.punchline: He can't figure out how to do it — the implied physical comedy of Mac failing at his own cool move before the confrontation deflates his authority
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy of Mac fumbling his own intimidation maneuver is a good payoff to his confident announcement. Classic setup-and-fail structure. Works better visually than it reads in transcript.

jokes.text: 'What a penis!' 'Like you wouldn't do such a thing?'
jokes.setup: Mac fumbles the gun-in-waistband move
jokes.punchline: Dennis mocks him ('What a penis!') but Mac's comeback ('Like you wouldn't do such a thing?') perfectly exposes Dennis's own ridiculousness — if Mac is a penis for trying, Dennis would do the same
jokes.explanation: Good dynamic between Mac and Dennis — Dennis's superiority is instantly undercut by Mac's knowing comeback. These two's mutual deflation of each other is at the heart of their relationship.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis's realization that Colin might not rob the same bar twice — 'Do you think this guy would be dumb enough to rob the same bar twice?' — followed immediately by their mutual agreement: 'Yeah, I do.' 'Me too.'
jokes.setup: They note that Fingers Bar (which Colin is visiting) has already been robbed — maybe he wouldn't come back
jokes.punchline: Despite the momentary hesitation suggesting doubt, both immediately confirm yes, they think he'd be that dumb — an instant mutual agreement that's both funny and reveals their low opinion of Colin
jokes.explanation: The beat pause before they both say 'yeah, I do / me too' is structurally clean — a moment of apparent reflection that collapses into their original prejudice. Good economy.

jokes.text: Mac to Colin: 'You seem like, uh, the cat who ate the canary.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are trying to seem casual while confronting their prime suspect
jokes.punchline: Mac using an obscure idiom ('cat who ate the canary') while trying to seem cool is both a character-specific detail (Mac's posturing) and funny because it's such an unusual choice of phrase
jokes.explanation: Mac's choice of idiom is odd enough to be funny — 'cat who ate the canary' is not what most people would naturally say, and Colin's confused 'Canary... No' response shows how out of place it is.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis fabricate a story that there's money left in the register that the thief missed, calling the thief a 'stupid asshole,' 'What a cock!', 'What an idiot! What a total idiot!'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are baiting Colin by pretending the thief missed money in the register
jokes.punchline: They pile on with increasingly enthusiastic insults about the 'stupid asshole' thief — which they know is Colin — escalating to 'cock,' 'boner,' 'schmuck' in rapid succession while Colin presumably tries to look neutral
jokes.explanation: The escalating insult list directed at Colin while he has to pretend not to be the person being described is classic irony-based comedy. The progression from 'stupid asshole' to 'cock' to 'boner' to 'schmuck' is funny in its enthusiasm. Mac and Dennis's delight in this trap is very in character.

jokes.text: On the way out of the bar, Mac and Dennis compliment Colin's appearance: 'You look spiffy, bro.' 'Yeah, you look good.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis have just baited Colin and are leaving
jokes.punchline: They pivot to genuinely complimenting his appearance on the way out — an odd, almost affectionate moment with the man they're setting up
jokes.explanation: The abrupt compliment is a funny tonal shift — these guys who just set up an elaborate trap are cheerfully complimenting his outfit. Suggests Mac and Dennis are oddly sincere about certain social niceties even when scheming.

jokes.text: Colin casually tells Mac and Dennis they should get a gun — 'I keep one on me at all times' — not knowing they already have one and are planning to catch him with it.
jokes.setup: Colin, the robbery suspect, advises Mac and Dennis to get a gun for protection
jokes.punchline: The irony that Colin — the man they're setting up — is advising them to arm themselves is rich; and Mac's reaction shot ('From now on, so will we') closes the trap
jokes.explanation: Good dramatic irony — Colin is completely unaware he's accelerating his own downfall. 'I keep one on me at all times' as a boast from the man about to be caught is nicely constructed. Mac's response ('From now on, so will we') lands as a great understated button.

jokes.text: In the dark bar, waiting for the robber, someone asks 'Did you just cock back the hammer, bro?'
jokes.setup: The gang is hiding in the darkened bar waiting for Colin to come rob it
jokes.punchline: In the tense stakeout atmosphere, one of them has cocked back the hammer of the loaded gun — confirming they are absolutely not qualified to be doing this
jokes.explanation: Good foreshadowing beat — the accidental cocking of the hammer in the dark establishes that someone is going to get shot. The casual tone of 'bro' in what should be a tense moment is very IASIP.

jokes.text: Dee reveals she didn't know about the gun: 'Wait a second. You guys have a gun?' Dennis says 'We are not shooting anybody tonight!' — which immediately invites speculation that they might.
jokes.setup: Dee is surprised they have a gun; Dennis emphatically states no one will be shot
jokes.punchline: Dennis protesting that no one will be shot is precisely the kind of dramatic irony that guarantees someone will be shot
jokes.explanation: Classic dramatic irony setup — 'we are NOT shooting anyone tonight' is essentially a guarantee that shooting will occur. The audience knows this, which makes it funny even before the shot is fired.

jokes.text: In the dark, Mac and Dennis argue about who should hold the gun: 'I should be holding the gun.' 'I have better...' 'I put this whole thing together.' 'I shot the log way more times!' 'I'm the one who has better aim than you!'
jokes.setup: In the middle of their stakeout, waiting for a potentially armed criminal
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis are bickering about gun custody like children arguing over a toy — 'I shot the log way more times!' as a credential is particularly absurd
jokes.explanation: 'I shot the log way more times!' is the callback that makes this joke excellent — it invokes their earlier childish log-shooting as a legitimate credential for handling a real dangerous situation. The whole argument perfectly captures their immaturity.

jokes.text: No, no! He's getting away! / Shoot him! / What? / Shoot him! / Shoot him in his face! / Shit!
jokes.setup: The intruder is getting away; Dee can't work the flashlight
jokes.punchline: The 'shoot him in his face!' instruction — immediately after all agreeing no one would shoot anyone — is a complete reversal of the safety agreement, and the specificity of 'in his face' is brutal and funny
jokes.explanation: The speed of the reversal from 'we are NOT shooting anyone' to 'SHOOT HIM IN HIS FACE' is excellent — it makes the earlier safety discussion completely hollow. 'In his face' is a great specific escalation. The callback payoff is clean and fast. Very quotable. This is a highlight of the episode.

jokes.text: Did you get him? / I'm shot! / Charlie? Oh, my God!
jokes.setup: A gun has fired in the dark bar during the confrontation
jokes.punchline: Mac's 'did you get him?' is immediately answered with 'I'm shot!' — the person shot is their own friend Charlie, not the intruder
jokes.explanation: The reveal that the person shot is Charlie — who has his own subplot with the gun — is a satisfying structural collision. 'Did you get him? / I'm shot!' is a clean, well-timed exchange. Dark and funny.

jokes.text: 'Charlie, I shot you in your head. I am so sorry.'
jokes.setup: Lights are on; it becomes clear Charlie has been shot in the head
jokes.punchline: Dennis's apology for shooting his friend in the head is delivered with the casualness of someone who knocked over a coffee — the tone is completely inappropriate for the severity of the act
jokes.explanation: 'Charlie, I shot you in your head. I am so sorry.' is a great line — the specificity ('in your head') followed by a totally inadequate 'I am so sorry' captures Dennis's sociopathic emotional range. His phrasing is oddly formal ('in your head' rather than 'in the head') which adds an additional layer of wrong-ness.

jokes.text: 'If I shot him in the head, he'd be dead.' Mac's immediate response to Dennis shooting Charlie in the head.
jokes.setup: Everyone is reacting to Charlie being shot in the head
jokes.punchline: Mac's cool-headed assessment ('if I shot him in the head, he'd be dead') is technically the wrong moment for logical reasoning — but it also implies Mac is better at shooting than Dennis, returning to their earlier rivalry
jokes.explanation: Mac using this moment to implicitly claim superior marksmanship is very funny — even with their friend bleeding, the rivalry continues. The deadpan logic ('if I shot him in the head, he'd be dead') is cold and funny.

jokes.text: Dennis refuses to put Charlie in his car because 'I don't wanna get blood stains all over the interior of my car.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has been shot and they need to get him to a hospital three blocks away
jokes.punchline: Dennis's objection to driving Charlie to the hospital is not concern about speed or capability — it's about his car's interior. His vanity overrides all human compassion.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best and most quintessentially Always Sunny jokes. Dennis just shot his best friend and his primary concern is blood on his car's interior. This is EXACTLY who Dennis is — a narcissist with no empathy dressed in concern for aesthetics. The character integration score approaches 9 because this joke could only come from Dennis: Mac would have different objections, Charlie wouldn't have a car. It's precise, it's dark, it's character-defining. Among the most quotable lines of the episode.

jokes.text: 'Get a trash bag. We'll put it over him.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has agreed to drive Charlie to the hospital but is concerned about blood stains
jokes.punchline: His solution is to cover the bleeding Charlie in a trash bag — not for warmth or pressure on the wound, but to protect the car upholstery
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'I don't want blood stains' to 'put a trash bag over him' is a perfect button on the previous joke. Dennis's solution is so practical and so wrong — he's not thinking about Charlie's welfare at all, only the upholstery. The trash bag as a medical intervention is simultaneously horrifying and hilarious. This and #59 form one of the episode's best two-beat sequences.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis's argument on the way to the hospital: 'You almost killed our best friend.' 'You guys told me to shoot Charlie!' then 'Then all of a sudden you told me to shoot him in the face!'
jokes.setup: In the aftermath of shooting Charlie, Mac blames Dennis
jokes.punchline: Dennis correctly notes that Mac told him to 'shoot him in his face' — which is true, making Mac's moral outrage completely hypocritical
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'shoot him in his face' works well — Dennis's defense is correct, which makes Mac's self-righteous framing even funnier. Good character work showing both of them avoiding accountability.

jokes.text: In the hospital, Dennis tells Charlie: 'But, Charlie, you were stealing from the bar. It was an honest mistake.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is in the hospital after being shot; they're reconciling
jokes.punchline: Dennis's framing of shooting Charlie as 'an honest mistake' because Charlie was stealing is a perfect piece of Dennis-logic — it inverts blame so thoroughly that the shooter is absolved and the theft victim becomes the guilty party
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'You were stealing from the bar. It was an honest mistake.' is a masterclass in character-specific rationalization. Dennis has constructed a world where shooting someone is forgivable if they had it coming — and delivers it with complete sincerity. The phrase 'honest mistake' applied to shooting someone in the head is the kind of linguistic perversion that IASIP does best. High quotability, strong character integration, clean structure.

jokes.text: Charlie explains his plan: he was going to stage the robbery to look like all the other robberies, collect insurance money, and thought it was 'the best idea I ever had.'
jokes.setup: The gang discovers Charlie stole their safe — not Colin
jokes.punchline: Charlie's insurance fraud scheme — which resulted in him getting shot in the head — is described with pride as his best idea ever. The gang's response ('that's really just goddamn ridiculous,' 'that is so dumb') followed by Mac's qualifier ('It might be the best idea you've ever had, but...') is perfect.
jokes.explanation: The twist that Charlie was the robber all along is funny, but the funnier joke is Mac's inadvertent compliment: 'It might be the best idea you've ever had, but...' — this is a savage indictment of Charlie's overall intelligence wrapped in a failed attempt at encouragement. The structure perfectly captures the gang's mutual incompetence: Charlie's grand scheme got him shot; Mac can't even deliver an insult cleanly.

jokes.text: In the hospital room, Dennis and Mac solemnly tell Charlie they've decided to get rid of the gun. The moment Dee leaves the room, Mac turns to Dennis: 'Tell me we're not getting rid of that gun.' 'No way!' 'Never.' 'Sweet.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis tell Charlie (and Dee) they're getting rid of the dangerous gun
jokes.punchline: The instant Dee exits, they reveal they were lying — with gleeful, conspiratorial speed. 'Never.' 'Sweet.' closes it perfectly.
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode button. The pattern has been established all episode — whenever these guys express responsibility about the gun, they immediately contradict themselves. This final beat delivers on that pattern with maximum economy: they waited for Dee to leave the room, then needed about three seconds to confirm they're keeping it. 'Never.' 'Sweet.' is a great closing exchange. Strong structural payoff to the episode's central joke.

jokes.text: I guess I'm just a sweet guy. / All right. Well, I'll see you tomorrow? / You will. / Okay. Good night. / Dream of me.
jokes.setup: Colin is confirming plans with Dee while having just robbed her bar
jokes.punchline: 'Dream of me' — the clichéd romantic sign-off from a man who robbed the bar of her friend group, completely unaware of how exposed he is
jokes.explanation: Colin's breezy 'dream of me' as a robber who's gotten away clean is good ironic character comedy. The '80s stereotype smooth talk applied to this situation is funny.

jokes.text: Final shot: Colin, clearly having just fled the bar, mutters to himself: 'Idiots.'
jokes.setup: Colin has just had the worst night — set up in a sting, nearly caught, someone got shot
jokes.punchline: His one-word dismissal of the entire gang as 'idiots' is the final joke — and while he's not wrong, he's also the one who keeps robbing bars and dating a woman with terrible friends. The word lands with great finality.
jokes.explanation: One word, maximum economy. 'Idiots.' from someone who just had to flee from a gang who accidentally shot their own friend is rich in irony. It's also technically correct, which makes it funnier. A clean, satisfying button to the episode.

tmdb_overview: The guys buy a gun after the bar's safe is stolen.
